title: Product Management Fundamentals
tagline: Find the right problem, decide what to build and measure the result, with practice in every module
summary: Learn the core skills of product management: discovery and user research, metrics and experiments, strategy and prioritisation, writing briefs, working with design and engineering, launching and ethical practice. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Product foundations
modules.summary: What a product manager does, how products create value and what makes a team successful.
modules.outcome: You can describe the product manager's role, distinguish outputs from outcomes and explain the product life cycle.
modules.intro: A product manager is responsible for making sure the team builds the right thing, for the right people, for the right reasons. It is a role of influence rather than authority: you rarely manage the people you depend on.

topics.title: What is a product, and what does a product manager do?
topics.html:
Definition

Product. Something that solves a problem for a group of people and that the organisation creates, improves and supports over time. It can be software, a physical item, a service or a platform.

The three circles
CircleQuestionOwned mainly by
UsersDo people need and love it?Product and design (user experience)
BusinessDoes it make or save money, or advance the mission?Product and business leaders
TechnologyCan we build and run it reliably?Engineering

A product manager works in the overlap of these circles. They are not the boss of designers or engineers; they are responsible for the outcome. Their main tools are research, clear thinking, writing, prioritising and persuading.

Typical responsibilities

  • Understand users and their problems.
  • Define the product vision and strategy.
  • Set goals and success metrics.
  • Prioritise what to build and what not to build.
  • Work with design and engineering to deliver.
  • Communicate with stakeholders and customers.
  • Learn from results and adjust.
Tip

A good PM says 'no' more often than 'yes', and always explains why.

Check what you just learned

1. A product manager mainly:
  • Decides what problem to solve and why (correct)
  • Writes all the code
  • Designs all screens
  • Approves salaries

The role is about direction and outcomes.
keyPoints: A PM works where user needs, business goals and technology meet.
The role is about outcomes, influence and prioritising.

topics.title: Output versus outcome
topics.html:
Shipping is not success
OutputOutcome
Launched dark modeEvening usage rose 12%
Wrote 30 help articlesSupport tickets fell 35%
Released version 2.0 on timeWeek-two retention rose from 42% to 48%

Teams that measure themselves by what they ship tend to build feature after feature. Teams that measure change in user behaviour and business results tend to build less, but better. Outcomes are harder to predict, which is why discovery and experiments matter.

Watch out

Be careful with vanity numbers such as downloads or page views that can rise without any real benefit to users. Ask whether a metric reflects value delivered.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is an outcome?
  • We shipped a new screen
  • Retention rose from 42% to 48% (correct)
  • We wrote 30 articles
  • We held 10 meetings

It measures change.
keyPoints: Outcomes are changes in behaviour and results; outputs are what you ship.
Aim for outcomes.

topics.title: The product life cycle and team
topics.html:
Stages
StageFocusTypical metrics
DiscoveryIs there a real problem and a promising idea?Interview insights, test results
Launch / earlyFind the first loyal usersActivation, early retention
GrowthReach more people efficientlyNew users, conversion, referrals
MaturityOptimise and defendMargin, retention, satisfaction
Decline / renewalReinvent or retireUsage trends, cost to serve

The best PM adjusts to the stage. Early on, speed of learning matters more than polish; at maturity, reliability and efficiency matter more.

Working with the team

  1. Share the problem, not just the solution, with engineers and designers.
  2. Involve them early in discovery.
  3. Be clear on priorities and the reasons behind them.
  4. Respect their expertise and time.
  5. Celebrate shared wins.
Tip

Engineers and designers often have the best ideas. Give them the problem and the goal, and let them surprise you.

It helps to remember that a product is never finished. Even a successful product is a bet that continues to need evidence: customers change, competitors respond and technology shifts. That is why product managers spend so much time on learning loops. Each release is a hypothesis about what will help users, and each result, whether a win or a disappointment, is information that improves the next bet.

Check what you just learned

1. Early in a product's life, what matters most?
  • Perfect polish
  • Cost cutting
  • Speed of learning (correct)
  • Maximum features

Learn what users want.

Key terms: flip and sort

Product
Something that solves a problem for users
Outcome
A change in behaviour or results
Output
What a team ships
Stakeholder
A person with an interest in the product
Discovery
Learning what to build
keyPoints: Focus changes with the life-cycle stage.
Share problems and goals with the team, not just solutions.

modules.title: Discovery and user research
modules.summary: Understand users and problems before deciding what to build.
modules.outcome: You can plan and run user interviews, describe a job to be done, synthesise findings and write a problem statement.
modules.intro: Discovery is how you reduce the risk of building something nobody wants. It means talking to people, watching what they do and looking at data, before committing months of work.

topics.title: Interviewing users
topics.html:
Good and bad interview questions
AvoidAsk
Would you use a progress report?Tell me about the last time you wondered whether you were improving.
Do you like our app?What did you do the last time you opened it?
Is the price fine?What have you paid for to learn a language before?
Wouldn't a leaderboard be fun?Tell me about a time you felt motivated to keep studying.

Running the conversation

  1. Explain that you are learning, not selling.
  2. Start with easy questions about their context.
  3. Ask about specific recent events.
  4. Follow up with 'Why?' and 'What happened next?'.
  5. Stay silent after questions and let them think.
  6. Record (with permission) or take careful notes.
  7. Thank them.

Aim for 5 to 10 interviews per question. Patterns appear quickly. After that, you will mostly hear repeats.

Watch out

Always get permission before recording, protect the personal data you collect and use it only for the purpose you explained.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a better question?
  • Would you use this?
  • Isn't it great?
  • Do you like my design?
  • Tell me about the last time you had this problem (correct)

Past behaviour reveals more.
keyPoints: Ask about specific past behaviour; avoid leading and hypothetical questions.
Get consent and protect data.

topics.title: Jobs to be done and personas
topics.html:
Definition

Job to be done. The progress a person is trying to make in a particular situation. People 'hire' products to make that progress.

Formula · A job statement

When I <situation>, I want to <motivation>, so I can <expected outcome>

When I have a few minutes on the bus, I want to practise speaking without feeling silly, so I can see real progress.

Why jobs help
Persona (who)Job (why)
Anita, 28, accountantShe wants to feel confident in a meeting with overseas clients
Rahul, 19, studentHe wants to pass a language test for study abroad

Two people who look different on paper may hire a product for the same job, and two similar people may have different jobs. Focusing on the job keeps teams from designing for averages.

Tip

A good job statement describes a situation and a motivation, not a solution.

Check what you just learned

1. A job statement should not contain:
  • A specific solution (correct)
  • A motivation
  • A situation
  • An outcome

Describe progress, not the answer.
keyPoints: A job is the progress a user wants in a situation.
Use the 'When I, I want to, so I can' form.

topics.title: Synthesising and defining the problem
topics.html:
A problem statement
PartExample
UserWorking adults learning a language on their phones
JobPractise in spare minutes and see progress
PainThey lose motivation as they cannot see improvement
Evidence58% do not return after day 7; 9 of 12 interviewees mentioned progress
OpportunityRaise week-two retention from 42% to 48%

Mix methods

  • Interviews tell you why.
  • Analytics tell you what and how many.
  • Usability tests show where people struggle.
  • Surveys test how common something is, after interviews tell you what to ask.

Common mistakes

  • Using one interview to decide.
  • Seeking only evidence that supports your idea.
  • Jumping straight to a solution.

Check what you just learned

1. Analytics mainly tell you:
  • Why users behave as they do
  • What and how many (correct)
  • What they dream
  • Nothing

Pair with interviews for why.

Key terms: flip and sort

Discovery
Research to decide what to build
JTBD
Jobs to be done
Synthesis
Turning raw data into insight
Usability test
Watching users try a product
Persona
A fictional user profile
keyPoints: Group notes into themes and quantify them.
Combine qualitative (why) and quantitative (how many) evidence.

modules.title: Metrics and experiments
modules.summary: Choose metrics that matter, read funnels and run fair experiments.
modules.outcome: You can define a North Star metric, build and read a funnel and judge an A/B test.
modules.intro: Metrics turn a product from a feeling into a conversation about evidence. Good ones focus the team; bad ones reward the wrong behaviour.

topics.title: Choosing metrics
topics.html:
Metric families
FamilyQuestionExample
AcquisitionHow do people find us?New installs, cost per install
ActivationDo they reach the first value?Share who finish lesson 1
RetentionDo they come back?Week-two retention
RevenueDo they pay?Conversion to paid, average revenue per user
ReferralDo they tell others?Invitations sent
Definition

North Star metric. The single measure that best captures the value your product delivers to users and that leads to business success, such as 'weekly active learners' or 'meals delivered per student per week'.

Good metrics are

  • Tied to user value, not vanity.
  • Understood by everyone.
  • Measured consistently.
  • Sensitive: they move when you improve the product.
  • Balanced by guardrails (such as quality or complaints) so you do not harm users.
Watch out

When a metric becomes a target, people may game it. Pair every key metric with a guardrail that would reveal harm.

Check what you just learned

1. A guardrail metric helps you avoid:
  • Using spreadsheets
  • Measuring anything
  • Gaming the main metric at users' expense (correct)
  • Experiments

Protects users.
keyPoints: Acquisition, activation, retention, revenue, referral.
A North Star metric reflects value to users; add guardrails.

topics.title: Funnels and retention
topics.html:
An example funnel
StepUsersFrom previousOf installs
Installed10,000-100%
Finished sign-up6,50065%65%
Completed lesson 14,20065%42%
Returned on day 71,90045%19%
Paid38020%3.8%

A funnel shows where people drop off. The biggest drop is not always the one to fix first: consider how many people it affects and how fixable it is. Here the step to paid is lowest in percent, but improving day-7 return affects many more people and feeds the later steps.

Formula · Retention

retention on day N = users still active on day N / users who started

If 1,900 of 4,200 who finished lesson 1 return on day 7, day-7 retention is 45%.

Tip

Look at cohorts: group users by the week they joined, and compare how each group behaves. It shows whether changes help.

Check what you just learned

1. Day-7 retention is:
  • Clicks
  • Revenue on day 7
  • Installs on day 7
  • Users active on day 7 / users who started (correct)

Return rate.
keyPoints: A funnel shows where users drop; consider size and fixability.
Compare cohorts to see whether changes help.

topics.title: Experiments
topics.html:
A hypothesis
PartExample
If weshow a weekly progress summary
thenweek-two retention will rise
becauseusers will see that they are improving
measured byretention, with unsubscribes as a guardrail

Read a test result

Change visitors and conversions for each version to see the rates and the lift.

Adjust Version A visitors, Version A converted, Version B visitors, Version B converted and see A conversion, B conversion, Lift of B over A change.

Watch out

With small samples, random chance can look like a win. Do not stop a test the moment B pulls ahead, and do not run many variants and pick the best without adjusting expectations. Professional teams use statistical tests; for this course, remember that bigger samples and longer tests give more reliable results.

Check what you just learned

1. Why decide the success rule before the test?
  • To avoid bending the result to fit what you hope (correct)
  • It is faster
  • It is a legal rule
  • To save money

Avoid fooling yourself.

Key terms: flip and sort

North Star metric
The key measure of delivered value
Funnel
A sequence of steps users take
Cohort
A group of users who started together
Guardrail
A metric that protects against harm
Hypothesis
A testable prediction
keyPoints: Hypothesis, metric, random split, enough time.
Small samples can mislead.

steps: Say which step you would work on first and why.

modules.title: Strategy, prioritisation and roadmaps
modules.summary: Set a vision, choose what to do first and communicate a roadmap without false promises.
modules.outcome: You can write a product vision, prioritise with RICE and build a Now-Next-Later roadmap.
modules.intro: A team can build anything; it cannot build everything. Strategy is the discipline of choosing, and a roadmap is how you communicate the choices.

topics.title: Vision and strategy
topics.html:
The hierarchy
LevelQuestionExample
VisionWhat world do we want to create?The easiest way for hostel students to get a trusted meal at any hour
StrategyHow will we win and what will we focus on?Win on reliability and trust before price and variety
Goals / OKRsWhat will we achieve this quarter?Raise weekly orders per student from 1.4 to 2.0
InitiativesWhat will we do?Launch order tracking; partner with five kitchens

A good strategy includes choices about what not to do. 'Do everything for everyone' is not a strategy. Choose a user, a problem and a way of being valuable that competitors will find hard to match.

Test your strategy

  • Could a competitor reasonably choose the opposite?
  • Does it help the team say no?
  • Is it based on evidence about users and the market?
  • Can you explain it in two minutes?
Tip

Write the strategy so that a new team member could use it to decide between two feature requests.

Check what you just learned

1. A good strategy includes:
  • Everything for everyone
  • Choices about what not to do (correct)
  • No goals
  • A long list

Focus comes from deliberate choices about what to skip.
keyPoints: Vision, strategy, goals and initiatives nest together.
Strategy includes what not to do.

topics.title: Prioritisation
topics.html:
Formula · RICE

score = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort

Progress dashboard: 8,000 users × impact 2 × confidence 0.8 / 2 person-months = 6,400.

RICE inputs
InputMeaningScale
ReachHow many users per period will it affect?A number
ImpactHow much will it move the goal for each user?0.25 minimal, 0.5 low, 1 medium, 2 high, 3 massive
ConfidenceHow sure are we of the estimates?0 to 1 (or percent)
EffortHow much work from the whole team?Person-months
Other methods
MethodUse
Value vs effortQuick 2x2 sorting
MoSCoWMust, should, could, won't for a release
KanoBasics, performance and delighters
Cost of delayWhere waiting loses most value
Watch out

A formula informs judgement; it does not replace it. Check the result against strategy, dependencies and risk, and be willing to override a score for a good reason you can explain.

Check what you just learned

1. In RICE, higher effort:
  • Raises the score
  • Has no effect
  • Lowers the score (correct)
  • Doubles reach

It is in the denominator.
keyPoints: RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort.
Scores inform judgement; they do not replace it.

topics.title: Roadmaps
topics.html:
A roadmap communicates direction and order. Roadmaps built on exact dates often break, damage trust and lead to building to a schedule rather than to outcomes.

Now / Next / Later
ColumnMeaningCertainty
NowIn progress this periodHigh
NextPlanned after; needs more detailMedium
LaterIdeas and opportunitiesLow

Good roadmap habits

  • Organise around problems and outcomes, not only features.
  • Be honest about uncertainty.
  • Share with stakeholders regularly and explain changes.
  • Link each item to a goal.
  • Remove items when the reason changes.

Common mistakes

  • Promising dates for uncertain work.
  • A long list of features with no goals.
  • Never updating the roadmap.

Check what you just learned

1. Items in 'Later' are:
  • Committed and detailed
  • Cancelled
  • Finished
  • Ideas with low certainty (correct)

They may change.

Key terms: flip and sort

Vision
The future you want to create
Strategy
A set of choices on where to focus
OKR
Objectives and key results
RICE
A prioritisation score
Roadmap
A communication of direction and order
keyPoints: Use Now, Next, Later to show order and certainty.
Link roadmap items to goals; avoid false date promises.

practical.title: Practical: prioritise ten ideas
steps: Compare with your gut and explain any difference.

questions.explanation: Focus comes from deliberate choices about what to skip.

modules.title: Building and launching
modules.summary: Turn a problem into a clear brief, work with the team and launch responsibly.
modules.outcome: You can write a product requirements document, work in iterations and run a launch checklist.
modules.intro: Discovery and strategy mean little unless the team can build and release safely. A PM supports this with clarity, quick decisions and good judgement about quality.

topics.title: Writing a clear brief
topics.html:
A one-page product requirements document (PRD)
SectionPurpose
ProblemWhy are we doing this? Evidence.
GoalWhat measurable change do we want?
In scope / out of scopeWhat we will and will not do
User stories or flowsHow it should work for users
Success metricsHow we will know it worked
Risks and open questionsWhat could go wrong; what we do not know yet

A brief should be short enough to be read and specific enough to build from. It is a conversation starter. The best ones are written with engineers and designers, not handed to them.

Writing rules

  1. Lead with the problem and the goal.
  2. Use plain words.
  3. Be explicit about what is out of scope.
  4. Give numbers for goals.
  5. Leave room for the team's solutions.
Tip

If the team can build the wrong thing from your brief, the brief is not clear enough.

Check what you just learned

1. A PRD should begin with:
  • The problem and goal (correct)
  • The code
  • The logo
  • The deadline only

Why before what.
keyPoints: A brief states the problem, goal, scope, flows, metrics and risks.
Keep it short and specific.

topics.title: Working with design and engineering
topics.html:
Healthy working habits
HabitWhy
Share the problem, not just the solutionBetter ideas, more ownership
Involve designers and engineers in discoveryFewer surprises
Hold regular short syncsSurface issues early
Make trade-offs visibleEveryone decides with the same facts
Decide quickly when blockedKeep momentum
Say thank you and credit othersTrust and morale

When scope is too large, trim scope instead of quality or the team's health. When time is short, ask which part is essential and which can follow. A good PM protects the team's focus from constant changes.

Common mistakes

  • Changing requirements mid-way without discussing the cost.
  • Treating engineers as order-takers.
  • Skipping testing to meet a date.
Watch out

Pressure to ship at all costs can lead to bugs, security gaps and burned-out teams. Quality and safety are part of the product.

Check what you just learned

1. When time is short you should first:
  • Cut testing
  • Trim scope to the essential (correct)
  • Hide the problem
  • Add features

Reduce scope, not quality.
keyPoints: Share problems, involve the team early and make trade-offs visible.
Trim scope before cutting quality.

topics.title: Launching and learning
topics.html:
A launch checklist

  1. Testing passed on main devices and conditions.
  2. Metrics and dashboards are live.
  3. Support and sales know what is changing.
  4. Documentation and messages are ready.
  5. A way to roll back quickly exists.
  6. Legal, privacy and accessibility checks are done.
  7. Owners and on-call people are named.
Release approaches
ApproachDescriptionBenefit
Staged rolloutRelease to a small share firstLimit harm if something breaks
BetaInvite selected usersEarly feedback
Feature flagSwitch a feature on or off without redeployingQuick rollback
Big bangEveryone at onceSimple, but risky

A launch is the start of learning. After release, watch the metrics and listen to support and users. Hold a short review after a few weeks: did the outcome change? What did we learn?

Tip

Plan the review before the launch: decide the date and the numbers you will check.

Check what you just learned

1. A staged rollout helps by:
  • Hiding the feature
  • Making launch slower for no reason
  • Limiting harm if something breaks (correct)
  • Avoiding metrics

Smaller risk.

Key terms: flip and sort

PRD
Product requirements document
Scope
What is included
Staged rollout
Release to a small share first
Feature flag
A switch to enable or disable a feature
Rollback
Returning to the previous version
keyPoints: Use a launch checklist and staged rollouts.
Review the outcome after release.

options: Is always slower for no benefit

modules.title: Leading, stakeholders and ethics
modules.summary: Influence without authority, communicate with stakeholders and build products responsibly.
modules.outcome: You can manage stakeholders, communicate trade-offs and apply basic ethical checks to product decisions.
modules.intro: Much of a PM's work is communication: aligning leaders, saying no kindly and ensuring the product does right by users and society.

topics.title: Stakeholders and communication
topics.html:
Typical stakeholders
GroupCares about
LeadershipStrategy, growth, risk
Sales and marketingCustomer promises, launch timing
SupportFewer tickets, clear changes
Legal and complianceRules and risk
Engineering and designClarity, quality, sustainable pace
UsersValue, trust, ease

Habits

  • Send short regular updates.
  • Share bad news early.
  • Tailor detail to the audience.
  • Write down decisions and the reasons.
  • Listen for the need behind a request.
Tip

When a stakeholder asks for a feature, ask 'What problem will this solve?' It turns a demand into a conversation about outcomes.

Check what you just learned

1. A good response to a feature request is to ask:
  • Who asked?
  • Is it cheap?
  • Why not earlier?
  • What problem will this solve? (correct)

Find the need.
keyPoints: Align stakeholders with decisions, evidence and trade-offs.
Ask what problem a request solves.

topics.title: Ethics, privacy and inclusion
topics.html:
Products affect real people. A PM has a duty to think about harm as well as benefit: privacy, fairness, safety, accessibility and the wellbeing of users, especially children and vulnerable groups.

Questions to ask
AreaQuestion
PrivacyDo we need this data? Do users understand and agree to how we use it?
FairnessCould this work worse for some groups?
SafetyCould it be misused? What is the worst that can happen?
AccessibilityCan people with disabilities use it?
HonestyAre we clear and truthful, or manipulating people with dark patterns?
WellbeingAre we encouraging healthy use or compulsive use?

Practical steps

  • Collect only the data you need.
  • Make consent clear and easy to withdraw.
  • Test with diverse users and with assistive technology.
  • Avoid deceptive design that tricks users into actions.
  • Escalate concerns and keep a record.
  • Follow the relevant laws and standards in the places you operate.
Watch out

If a product decision would make you uncomfortable explaining to the people affected, stop and rethink it.

Check what you just learned

1. A dark pattern is:
  • Design that tricks users into actions (correct)
  • A theme
  • A style guide
  • A colour

It is deceptive.
keyPoints: Consider privacy, fairness, safety, accessibility and honesty.
Avoid dark patterns and collect only needed data.

topics.title: Growing as a product person
topics.html:
Skills to build
SkillHow to practise
Customer empathyTalk to users every week
Analytical thinkingRead dashboards; run small analyses in a spreadsheet
WritingWrite briefs and updates and ask for feedback
PrioritisationPractise scoring and defending choices
CommunicationPresent to different audiences
Technical fluencyLearn how your product is built at a basic level
LeadershipHelp others succeed

There are many routes into product work: from engineering, design, marketing, operations, analysis or study. What employers value is evidence that you can find problems, make choices and get things done with others. A small project you led, even for a club, counts.

Starter projects

  • Redesign a school process and measure the change.
  • Run interviews for a local business and write recommendations.
  • Write a product brief for an app you use and ask for feedback.
  • Build a small prototype with a no-code tool and test it with five people.
Tip

Keep a portfolio of one-page briefs and what you learned. It shows how you think.

Check what you just learned

1. A good way to build PM skill is to:
  • Wait for a job
  • Run small projects and write about them (correct)
  • Avoid users
  • Memorise terms only

Practice and evidence.

Key terms: flip and sort

Stakeholder
A person affected by or interested in the product
Dark pattern
Design that tricks users
Accessibility
Usable by people with disabilities
Privacy
Control over personal information
Trade-off
Giving up one thing to gain another
keyPoints: Build empathy, analysis, writing, prioritising and communication.
Show your thinking with small real projects.
